CausalChain: EMT -> Loss of miR-200 -> Upregulation of ZEB1 -> Acquisition of mesenchymal, stem-like properties and chemoresistance -> Exosome-mediated miRNA transfer -> Engineered exosomes delivering miR-200 mimics + DNMT inhibitor with targeting ligands -> Suppression of ZEB1 -> Reversion of EMT to MET -> Decreased stemness and increased chemosensitivity
Hypothesis: Engineered exosomes co-loaded with miR-200 family mimics and a DNMT inhibitor, and functionalized with cancer-targeting ligands, can effectively reverse EMT-induced drug resistance in cancer by suppressing ZEB1 expression. This dual-targeted approach is expected to re-establish miR-200 homeostasis, overcome epigenetic roadblocks, revert EMT to MET, reduce cancer stem-like properties, and restore chemosensitivity, thereby overcoming a critical limitation observed with miR-200 monotherapy in vivo.
Abstract: In this study, we propose a novel therapeutic strategy that leverages engineered exosomes as highly specific delivery vehicles loaded with a dual payload: miR-200 family mimics and a complementary DNMT inhibitor. Building upon the established causal chain linking epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), loss of miR-200, upregulation of ZEB1, and the acquisition of mesenchymal and stem-like properties leading to drug resistance, our approach additionally addresses the limitation observed with miR-200 delivery alone. By functionalizing the exosome surface with cancer cell-targeting ligands, we aim to enhance tumor-specific uptake, ensuring efficient restoration of intracellular miR-200 levels, robust suppression of ZEB1, and ultimately the reversion of EMT to MET. This integrated strategy is designed to decrease cancer stemness and restore chemosensitivity, representing a significant advancement over current miR-200-based interventions.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused solely on the delivery of miR-200 mimics via engineered exosomes to suppress ZEB1 and reverse EMT-induced drug resistance. The revised hypothesis incorporates an additional epigenetic modulator (DNMT inhibitor) to address the observed need for combination treatment (as evidenced by miR-200b requiring DNMT inhibition to affect metastasis in vivo). Furthermore, the new strategy includes the engineering of exosome surfaces with cancer-specific targeting ligands to enhance delivery specificity and efficacy. This evolution retains the original causal chain while integrating contemporary technological advancements to improve the practical implementability and potential clinical impact of the approach.
